It felt like both of those major changes hit me all at once, and I've been struggling ever since.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned the symptoms started after the changes at work and your child leaving for college; can you describe if there was a period where you felt numb or disconnected right after these events occurred, before developing the overwhelming and irritable feelings you're experiencing now?\n\nPatient: I don't really recall feeling numb or disconnected right after the changes happened. From the very beginning, I just felt incredibly stressed and overwhelmed, and I started overreacting and pulling back almost immediately.\n\nDoctor: Did you experience any significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning immediately after the changes, or did this develop more gradually over the four months?\n\nPatient: The problems actually started pretty quickly, within just a few weeks of the changes, rather than developing gradually. Right away, I started pulling back from friends, arguing with my wife, and my supervisor at work noticed my irritability and lack of engagement. These struggles have been going on pretty consistently for the last four months.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your symptoms started shortly after significant life changes and have persisted for four months; can you tell me if there was an initial period, however brief, where you experienced significant distress or impairment that seemed to be directly in response to these changes, before your current pattern of feeling overwhelmed and irritable became the dominant experience?\n\nPatient: No, there wasn't really a different phase—it hit me almost immediately. Within just a few weeks of the work reorganization and my youngest leaving, I experienced a sharp shift where I immediately started pulling back from friends, arguing with my wife, and feeling unable to get a handle on things. That same pattern of feeling overwhelmed and irritable has just persisted over the last four months.\n\nDoctor: Did you have any period, no matter how brief, where you felt a sense of intense emotional pain, horror, or helplessness directly related to the work reassignment or your child leaving for college, before the overwhelming and irritability became your main issue?\n\nPatient: No, I didn't experience any feelings of horror or that kind of intense helplessness. For me, it has really just been about feeling incredibly overwhelmed, stressed, and irritable, and like I can't get my footing with all these sudden changes.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any other significant life changes or stressors, aside from the work reassignment and your child leaving for college, that might have contributed to your current feelings of being overwhelmed and irritable?\n\nPatient: No, there haven't been any other major life changes or stressors. It really is just the combination of the work transition and the quiet house after our youngest left that has thrown everything off balance. Nothing else comes to mind.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced significant fatigue or a marked decrease in your mental and physical stamina since these changes occurred, which is not solely explained by your irritability or feeling overwhelmed?\n\nPatient: I haven't really noticed a major drop in my physical energy or extreme fatigue itself. Instead, I just feel mentally overwhelmed and unmotivated, and I completely lack the drive to take on anything extra right now.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any persistent and significant problems with your sleep patterns, such as insomnia or hypersomnia, since you started feeling overwhelmed and irritable?\n\nPatient: I haven't really noticed any major changes or significant problems with my sleep. For the most part, I've been sleeping about the same as I usually do.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned ducking calls from friends and hiding out in the garage; can you tell me more about what you're avoiding or trying to escape from when you do these things?\n\nPatient: I’m mostly trying to escape that overwhelming feeling of how upside down everything is and my own tendency to snap at people. Hiding out in the garage and avoiding my friends feels a lot easier than pretending everything is fine or trying to explain why I'm struggling so much to adapt. Right now, withdrawing just feels like the only way to avoid dealing with how out of depth I feel.\n\nDoctor: When you're hiding out in the garage or avoiding social interactions, are you specifically trying to avoid reminders of the stressful life changes, such as your work reassignment or your child leaving for college, or is it more about avoiding the feelings of overwhelm and irritability themselves?\n\nPatient: It's definitely more about avoiding the feelings of overwhelm and irritability themselves. I'm not trying to avoid specific reminders of work or my kid being gone; I'm just hiding out in the garage to escape how upside down everything feels because I don't know how to deal with it.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there was a specific aspect of the work reassignment or your child leaving for college that you felt was particularly traumatic, frightening, or threatening, which might have triggered your current state of feeling overwhelmed and irritable?\n\nPatient: No, it wasn't traumatic or frightening in a safety sense—as an EMT, I'm used to handling emergencies on the job. It's more that the sudden, cumulative loss of my predictable routine, the chaotic city shifts, and the quietness of the empty nest completely unmoored me. It has left me feeling completely unmoored and unsure of who I am now that the house is so quiet.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the feelings of being overwhelmed and irritable are primarily in response to the loss of your previous role and routine, or if they are more about the difficulty in adapting to the new demands and responsibilities of your reassignment and life changes?\n\nPatient: It’s really a combination of both. Losing my predictable rural routine and the lively home with my kids has left me feeling completely unmoored, while the unpredictable overtime and faster pace of the city shifts make it incredibly hard to adapt and find my footing.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instances where you felt like you were able to manage or cope with the stressors of your work reassignment and your child leaving for college without feeling overwhelmed, or has it been a consistent struggle from the beginning?\n\nPatient: It has been a consistent struggle right from the start. At the same time, the house went completely quiet after our youngest left for college, leaving my wife and me as empty nesters. Losing my usual routines like fishing, woodworking, and church activities made me feel unmoored, which is why I've been snapping at my wife and hiding out in the garage.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the duration and intensity of your feelings of being overwhelmed and irritable have remained relatively consistent since the onset, or have you noticed any fluctuations that might be tied to specific aspects of your work reassignment or life as an empty nester?\n\nPatient: Yes, they’ve been pretty consistent over the last four months, though the intensity definitely spikes when I'm dealing with the unpredictable city shifts or when the quietness of the empty house really hits me. I honestly believe that if I could get back to my old rural schedule or if home felt more like it used to, these feelings would ease up within a few months.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your current feelings of being overwhelmed and irritable would significantly improve if the stressful life changes, such as the work reassignment and your child leaving for college, were somehow reversed or resolved?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. I really believe that if I could go back to my old rural schedule or if things at home felt more like they used to, this rough patch would ease up within a few months. My struggles feel directly tied to these specific transitions, so getting that familiarity back would make a huge difference.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your feelings of overwhelm and irritability are primarily a result of the significant life changes you've experienced, or do you believe there's an underlying issue that these changes have exacerbated?\n\nPatient: I definitely believe these feelings are directly tied to the recent major life changes rather than any underlying issue. If things went back to my old rural schedule or if our home routines felt more normal, I'm confident this rough patch would ease up within a few months. It really is just about trying to adapt to everything turning upside down at once.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any decrease in interest or pleasure in activities that you normally enjoy, aside from feeling overwhelmed and irritable?"

Right now, withdrawing just feels like the only way to avoid dealing with how out of depth I feel.\n\nDoctor: When you're hiding out in the garage or avoiding social interactions, are you specifically trying to avoid reminders of the stressful life changes, such as your work reassignment or your child leaving for college, or is it more about avoiding the feelings of overwhelm and irritability themselves?\n\nPatient: It's definitely more about avoiding the feelings of overwhelm and irritability themselves. I'm not trying to avoid specific reminders of work or my kid being gone; I'm just hiding out in the garage to escape how upside down everything feels because I don't know how to deal with it.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there was a specific aspect of the work reassignment or your child leaving for college that you felt was particularly traumatic, frightening, or threatening, which might have triggered your current state of feeling overwhelmed and irritable?\n\nPatient: No, it wasn't traumatic or frightening in a safety sense—as an EMT, I'm used to handling emergencies on the job. It's more that the sudden, cumulative loss of my predictable routine, the chaotic city shifts, and the quietness of the empty nest completely unmoored me. I just feel unable to adapt to how upside down everything became all at once.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned the work reassignment and your child leaving for college as significant stressors; can you clarify if either of these events involved a sense of loss of control or a dramatic change in your role or identity that might be contributing to your feelings of being overwhelmed?\n\nPatient: Yes, both of them definitely hit my sense of control and identity hard. The shift to unpredictable city hours took away my control over my daily routine, while becoming an empty nester stripped away my daily role as an active father. It has left me feeling completely unmoored and unsure of who I am now that the house is so quiet.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the feelings of being overwhelmed and irritable are primarily in response to the loss of your previous role and routine, or if they are more about the difficulty in adapting to the new demands and responsibilities of your reassignment and life changes?\n\nPatient: It’s really a combination of both. Losing my predictable rural routine and the lively home with my kids has left me feeling completely unmoored, while the unpredictable overtime and faster pace of the city shifts make it incredibly hard to adapt and find my footing.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instances where you felt like you were able to manage or cope with the stressors of your work reassignment and your child leaving for college without feeling overwhelmed, or has it been a consistent struggle from the beginning?\n\nPatient: It has been a consistent struggle right from the start. Within a few weeks of the work transition and the house going quiet, I felt completely overwhelmed, and I haven't had any real breaks or moments where I felt like I was managing well. It has just been a continuous effort to try and get my feet back under me.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there were any specific aspects of the work reassignment or your child leaving for college that you felt were particularly stressful or challenging to adapt to, which might have contributed to your current state of feeling overwhelmed and irritable?\n\nPatient: The most challenging part was moving from my predictable 24-on/48-off rural schedule to an unpredictable urban rotation with sudden overtime, which completely threw off my daily rhythm. At the same time, the house went completely quiet after our youngest left for college, leaving my wife and me as empty nesters. Losing my usual routines like fishing, woodworking, and church activities made me feel unmoored, which is why I've been snapping at my wife and hiding out in the garage.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the duration and intensity of your feelings of being overwhelmed and irritable have remained relatively consistent since the onset, or have you noticed any fluctuations that might be tied to specific aspects of your work reassignment or life as an empty nester?\n\nPatient: Yes, they’ve been pretty consistent over the last four months, though the intensity definitely spikes when I'm dealing with the unpredictable city shifts or when the quietness of the empty house really hits me. I honestly believe that if I could get back to my old rural schedule or if home felt more like it used to, these feelings would ease up within a few months.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your current feelings of being overwhelmed and irritable would significantly improve if the stressful life changes, such as the work reassignment and your child leaving for college, were somehow reversed or resolved?\n\nPatient: Yes, absolutely. If things went back to my old rural schedule or if our home routines felt more normal, I'm confident this rough patch would ease up within a few months. It really is just about trying to adapt to everything turning upside down at once.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any decrease in interest or pleasure in activities that you normally enjoy, aside from feeling overwhelmed and irritable?\n\nPatient: Yes, I've definitely lost interest and stopped participating in the things I used to love. Now, I just spend almost all of my free time isolating alone in the garage.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about what specifically made you lose interest in activities like fishing, woodworking, and church, which you used to enjoy, and is this lack of interest something that you feel is directly related to your current feelings of being overwhelmed and irritable?\n\nPatient: Yes, it is directly tied to feeling so overwhelmed and unmoored by the sudden changes. The unpredictable city shifts and the quiet empty nest completely disrupted my routines, leaving me too exhausted and irritable to face friends or go to church. Instead of doing the things I used to enjoy, I just end up retreating to the garage because I feel too upside down to deal with any of it.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe any specific situations or reminders of the life changes that you're actively trying to avoid when you retreat to the garage, and how these avoidance behaviors have impacted your daily life and relationships?"

That same pattern of feeling overwhelmed and irritable has just persisted over the last four months.\n\nDoctor: Did you have any period, no matter how brief, where you felt a sense of intense emotional pain, horror, or helplessness directly related to the work reassignment or your child leaving for college, before the overwhelming and irritability became your main issue?\n\nPatient: No, I didn't experience any feelings of horror or that kind of intense helplessness. For me, it has really just been about feeling incredibly overwhelmed, stressed, and irritable, and like I can't get my footing with all these sudden changes.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any other significant life changes or stressors, aside from the work reassignment and your child leaving for college, that might have contributed to your current feelings of being overwhelmed and irritable?\n\nPatient: No, there haven't been any other major life changes or stressors. It really is just the combination of the work transition and the quiet house after our youngest left that has thrown everything off balance. Nothing else comes to mind.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced significant fatigue or a marked decrease in your mental and physical stamina since these changes occurred, which is not solely explained by your irritability or feeling overwhelmed?\n\nPatient: I haven't really noticed a major drop in my physical energy or extreme fatigue itself. For the most part, I've been sleeping about the same as I usually do.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned ducking calls from friends and hiding out in the garage; can you tell me more about what you're avoiding or trying to escape from when you do these things?\n\nPatient: I’m mostly trying to escape that overwhelming feeling of how upside down everything is and my own tendency to snap at people. Hiding out in the garage and avoiding my friends feels a lot easier than pretending everything is fine or trying to explain why I'm struggling so much to adapt. I'm even dragging my feet at work because everything suddenly feels so upside down.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever feel detached from yourself or the world around you, as if you're observing things from outside your body or like you're in a dream?\n\nPatient: No, I don't feel detached from myself or like I'm in a dream. It's more that I feel way too plugged into the stress, just constantly overwhelmed and irritable with everything that's changed.\n\nDoctor: Can you estimate how long you've been feeling this overwhelmed and irritable, and was there a specific event or time when these feelings started after the changes at work and home?\n\nPatient: These feelings have been going on for about four months now. They started within just a few weeks of the double whammy of me being reassigned to the city EMS shifts and our youngest leaving for college, which left the house incredibly quiet. It felt like both of those major changes hit me all at once, and I've been struggling ever since.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned the symptoms started after the changes at work and your child leaving for college; can you describe if there was a period where you felt numb or disconnected right after these events occurred, before developing the overwhelming and irritable feelings you're experiencing now?\n\nPatient: I don't really recall feeling numb or disconnected right after the changes happened. From the very beginning, I just felt incredibly stressed and overwhelmed, and I started overreacting and pulling back almost immediately.\n\nDoctor: Did you experience any significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning immediately after the changes, or did this develop more gradually over the four months?\n\nPatient: The problems actually started pretty quickly, within just a few weeks of the changes, rather than developing gradually. Within just a few weeks of the work reorganization and my youngest leaving, I experienced a sharp shift where I immediately started pulling back from friends, arguing with my wife, and feeling unable to get a handle on things. I'm not trying to avoid specific reminders of work or my kid being gone; I'm just hiding out in the garage to escape how upside down everything feels because I don't know how to deal with it.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there was a specific aspect of the work reassignment or your child leaving for college that you felt was particularly traumatic, frightening, or threatening, which might have triggered your current state of feeling overwhelmed and irritable?\n\nPatient: No, it wasn't traumatic or frightening in a safety sense—as an EMT, I'm used to handling emergencies on the job. It's more that the sudden, cumulative loss of my predictable routine, the chaotic city shifts, and the quietness of the empty nest completely unmoored me. I just feel unable to adapt to how upside down everything became all at once.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned the work reassignment and your child leaving for college as significant stressors; can you clarify if either of these events involved a sense of loss of control or a dramatic change in your role or identity that might be contributing to your feelings of being overwhelmed?\n\nPatient: Yes, both of them definitely hit my sense of control and identity hard. The shift to unpredictable city hours took away my control over my daily routine, while becoming an empty nester stripped away my daily role as an active father. It has left me feeling completely unmoored and unsure of who I am now that the house is so quiet.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the feelings of being overwhelmed and irritable are primarily in response to the loss of your previous role and routine, or if they are more about the difficulty in adapting to the new demands and responsibilities of your reassignment and life changes?\n\nPatient: It’s really a combination of both. Losing my predictable rural routine and the lively home with my kids has left me feeling completely unmoored, while the unpredictable overtime and faster pace of the city shifts make it incredibly hard to adapt and find my footing.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any instances where you felt like you were able to manage or cope with the stressors of your work reassignment and your child leaving for college without feeling overwhelmed, or has it been a consistent struggle from the beginning?\n\nPatient: It has been a consistent struggle right from the start. It's more that the sudden, cumulative loss of my predictable routine, the chaotic city shifts, and the quietness of the empty nest completely unmoored me. I just feel unable to adapt to how upside down everything became all at once.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned the work reassignment and your child leaving for college as significant stressors; can you clarify if either of these events involved a sense of loss of control or a dramatic change in your role or identity that might be contributing to your feelings of being overwhelmed?\n\nPatient: Yes, both of them definitely hit my sense of control and identity hard. The shift to unpredictable city hours took away my control over my daily routine, while becoming an empty nester stripped away my daily role as an active father. It has left me feeling completely unmoored and unsure of who I am now that the house is so quiet.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if the feelings of being overwhelmed and irritable are primarily in response to the loss of your previous role and routine, or if they are more about the difficulty in adapting to the new demands and responsibilities of your reassignment and life changes?\n\nPatient: It’s really a combination of both.
